items.title: Bob Cranshaw interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995
items.q: I was invited to play. I mean I think back — Milt Hinton allowed me to play with Bing Crosby. ... And at Lincoln Center, I walked in to play the bass with Bing Crosby

ctx.x: I want to ask you a couple of more questions here. Where is jazz going and/or where does it need to go?

It’s hard to say because now we find out that jazz can make money. Before, there was money being made we didn’t realize it, we didn’t get most of it, but you know, we wanted to play. I say now when I go in, when I used to play in the pit and do Broadway shows, I always wondered, I tell musicians, because I’m working a lot for the musician’s union, not as a representative but as a person who was plugged in to the system by no fault of mine. I got plugged into the system and now I’m getting back I get a large…

guys coming out of the schools and so forth but I think that management and the music business has taken another look at it and said — hmmm, people are starting to like jazz. All those commercials I hear, everything is jazz now you know. And it’s a money making situation and most of the kids have no idea, they’re not in touch with the culture. With Josh Redman and so forth, Josh never has the time to spend with some older players or to see the older players, because they’re already moved aside, because of money…
